tagline: How a holy God can live among an unholy people: sacrifice, priesthood, purity, and a whole life set apart for him and for the neighbor.
overview:
Leviticus begins at the exact moment Exodus ends. The tabernacle has been set up, the cloud of God's glory has filled it, and Moses cannot go in. The book's first line answers that problem: the LORD calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and begins to explain how people may come near. What follows is the Bible's fullest account of sacrifice, priesthood, ritual purity, sacred time, and holiness in daily life. There are five kinds of offering, the ordination of Aaron and his sons, laws about food, childbirth, skin disease, and bodily discharges, the yearly Day of Atonement, and a long call to holiness that reaches into farming, business, sex, the courts, and the treatment of immigrants and the poor.

Many readers stall here, because the detail is dense and the world is unfamiliar. But Leviticus is answering one of the Bible's central questions: how can a holy God dwell in the middle of a people who are not holy without destroying them? Its answer is not that sin and death don't matter. It is that God himself provides a way, through blood, priesthood, washing, and an ordered common life, for a forgiven people to live near him. The book's most famous command, “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (19:2), stands only a few verses from its other famous line, “love your neighbor as yourself” (19:18). Leviticus will not separate worship from ethics.

For Christians it is the dictionary behind the New Testament's language about Jesus: sacrifice, atonement, high priest, clean and unclean, the veil, the blood. The Letter to the Hebrews can hardly be read without it. In Judaism, after the temple and its sacrifices ended in AD 70, the book remained central, reread through prayer, study, and deeds of kindness, and its food and purity laws continue to shape Jewish life.
author:
Leviticus names no author, but it presents nearly everything in it as speech from the LORD to Moses, sometimes to Moses and Aaron together, at Mount Sinai (1:1; 26:46; 27:34). Jewish and Christian tradition has accordingly counted it among the five books of Moses, and in the Gospels Jesus sends a healed leper to offer what Moses commanded for his cleansing (Mark 1:44), referring to the law of Leviticus 14 as Moses' law. Many conservative scholars, Gordon Wenham among them in his 1979 commentary, argue that the book's substance goes back to Moses and the wilderness period, whatever later editing it received.

Since the nineteenth century most critical scholars have assigned Leviticus to the Priestly source, one of the strands the documentary hypothesis finds woven through the first five books, and have treated chapters 17 to 26 as a distinct collection called the Holiness Code, named for its refrain about being holy as the LORD is holy. Opinion within that approach has shifted. Older critics thought the Holiness Code was earlier and was absorbed by the Priestly writers; Jacob Milgrom and Israel Knohl argued the reverse, that a later Holiness school edited and extended the Priestly material. Readers across these views agree that the book preserves the ritual knowledge of Israel's priesthood, knowledge that priestly families guarded and handed down with great care.
date:
The date follows the authorship question. Read as Mosaic, the book comes from the wilderness period just after the exodus, which is itself dated in two main ways: about 1446 BC, from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1, or in the thirteenth century BC, often linked with the store city Rameses named in Exodus 1:11.

Julius Wellhausen's influential reconstruction in the late nineteenth century placed the Priestly writing in or after the Babylonian exile, in the sixth or fifth century BC, as the charter of the rebuilt temple community. Other scholars, including Yehezkel Kaufmann and Jacob Milgrom, argued that the priestly laws are largely earlier than the exile, pointing to linguistic studies that find their Hebrew older than the language of Ezekiel, and to the fact that the laws assume a wilderness camp and a portable tent rather than the Jerusalem temple. Even a late written form can preserve far older ritual practice. Within the story itself the time covered is short: the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year after the exodus (Exodus 40:17), and Numbers opens on the first day of the second month (Numbers 1:1), so Leviticus fills about one month at Sinai.
setting:
The whole book is set at Mount Sinai, in the wilderness south of Canaan (the mountain's exact location is debated), where Israel camped for about a year after leaving Egypt. The people have received the covenant (Exodus 19 to 24), broken it with the golden calf (Exodus 32), been restored (Exodus 34), and built the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary with a courtyard, a bronze altar, and an inner room holding the ark. Leviticus pictures a camp arranged around that tent, with priests from Aaron's family serving at its altar.

Israel's neighbors all offered sacrifices, kept priesthoods, and practiced purification. Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast, from the late second millennium BC, name offerings with terms close to the Hebrew ones, and Hittite ritual texts describe driving away an animal to carry off plague or impurity, rites often compared with the scapegoat of Leviticus 16. Egyptian temples served the statues of their gods with daily meals and washings. Leviticus shares the vocabulary of that world but reshapes it. There is no image of God, and although the old language of offerings as God's food survives (3:11; 21:6), nothing in the book suggests that God needs feeding. The laws come as the words of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. The book also names practices Israel must refuse, among them child sacrifice to Molech (18:21; 20:2-5) and consulting mediums (19:31).
purpose:
Leviticus was written to teach Israel how to live with God in their midst. Its first audience was the priests, who had to know the procedures, and early Jewish tradition called the book the instruction of the priests (Torat Kohanim). Yet most of it is addressed to the whole people. Chapter after chapter opens with the charge, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them”, and the priests' own task is to “distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean” and to teach Israel accordingly (10:10-11). The goal of it all is stated in the covenant promise near the end: “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (26:12).

For later readers the book did more. Its warnings that the land would vomit out a people who defiled it (18:28; 20:22) explained the exile to those who lived through it, and its promise that God would remember his covenant even in the land of their enemies (26:44-45) gave them ground to hope.
story:
Leviticus is the middle book of the five books of Moses and the hinge between Exodus and Numbers. Genesis tells how humanity was driven from God's presence in Eden. Exodus tells how God rescued Israel from Egypt and came to dwell among them in the tabernacle. Leviticus explains how that dwelling can last. Numbers then takes the ordered camp out into the wilderness toward Canaan, and Deuteronomy restates the law on the edge of the land.

The book's patterns run through the rest of Scripture. The temple of Solomon carries on the tabernacle's worship. The prophets condemn sacrifice offered without justice (Isaiah 1; Amos 5), not because Leviticus was wrong but because Israel had split what it joined. Ezekiel, a priest, draws heavily on the book's language in his indictments and his vision of a new temple. And the Day of Atonement, the scapegoat, the Jubilee, and the call to holiness all return in the New Testament.
christ:
The New Testament reads Leviticus in the light of Jesus more closely than almost any other Old Testament book. Hebrews argues that Christ is the great high priest who entered not a sanctuary made with hands but heaven itself, with his own blood, once for all (Hebrews 9:11-14, 24-28), and that the Day of Atonement's yearly repetition showed that animal blood could not finally take away sins (Hebrews 10:1-4). Paul says God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice, using the Greek word that the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses for the mercy seat on the ark (Romans 3:25). Hebrews 13:11-12 compares the sin offering burned outside the camp with Jesus suffering outside the city gate.

In the Gospels Jesus touches the unclean, a leper and a woman with a long flow of blood, and instead of contracting their impurity he makes them clean (Mark 1:40-45; 5:25-34), while still sending the healed man to the priest with the offering Leviticus required. He names “love your neighbor as yourself” as the second great commandment (Mark 12:31), and 1 Peter 1:16 repeats the call to be holy as God is holy. The church has read all this as fulfillment rather than cancellation. The sacrifices and purity laws pointed toward a cleansing and nearness that Christ provides, which is why Christians do not offer animals and why most do not keep the food laws (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
reading:
Leviticus is mostly instruction: ritual procedures, case laws (if a person does this, then that), and lists, broken by two short narratives (chapters 8 to 10 and 24:10-23). Read it as you would the working rules of a sacred house, asking what each rule assumes about God, sin, life, and death.

Three misreadings are common. The first is that Israel earned God's favor by sacrifice; but the book is given to a people already rescued from Egypt (11:45; 26:13), and sacrifice is God's provision for keeping that relationship whole. The second is that unclean means sinful. Much impurity came from ordinary and even good things, such as childbirth, burying the dead, or a normal bodily discharge, and it was removed by time and washing; sin and impurity overlap but are not the same. The third is treating the laws as random taboos. Scholars have offered several explanations: the anthropologist Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), argued that clean animals are those that fit their category completely, so the laws teach wholeness; Jacob Milgrom argued that impurity is bound up with death and the laws train Israel to choose life; others stress separation from the practices of Canaan, or health.

Christians also differ on how the law applies now. A long tradition, found in Thomas Aquinas and in the Reformation confessions, distinguishes moral, ceremonial, and civil laws and holds that only the moral law binds believers directly. Others read the whole law as fulfilled in Christ and brought to believers through his teaching. Both take Leviticus as Christian Scripture.

structure.title: The offerings
structure.summary: Five kinds of offering (burnt, grain, peace, sin or purification, and guilt or reparation), first described from the worshiper's side and then as instructions for the priests who handle them.

structure.title: The priests ordained
structure.summary: Moses ordains Aaron and his sons over seven days. On the eighth day God's glory appears and fire consumes the offering, and then Nadab and Abihu die for offering unauthorized fire.

structure.title: Clean and unclean
structure.summary: Laws on food, childbirth, skin diseases and mold, and bodily discharges, with the rites that restore an unclean person to the community and the sanctuary.

structure.title: The Day of Atonement
structure.summary: Once a year the high priest enters the Most Holy Place to cleanse the sanctuary of Israel's impurities, and a live goat carries the people's sins away into the wilderness.

structure.title: Holiness in all of life
structure.summary: The Holiness Code: blood, sexual relations, love of neighbor, penalties, the holiness of priests and offerings, the yearly feasts, the Sabbath year and Jubilee, and the covenant's blessings and curses.

structure.title: Vows and dedications
structure.summary: Rules for dedicating people, animals, houses, and fields to the LORD, for redeeming them, and for the tithe, closing the book with a note that these commands were given at Sinai.

themes.title: Holiness
themes.body: The Hebrew word qadosh, holy, marks what belongs to God and is set apart from common use. God is holy in his otherness and his moral purity, and his holiness spreads outward from the Most Holy Place to the priests, the people, their calendar, and their land. The refrain “be holy, because I am holy” (11:44) is not a call to religious performance but to a whole life that matches the God who lives among them.

themes.title: God's presence among his people
themes.body: Everything in the book assumes that God actually lives in the middle of the camp. That is Israel's greatest gift and its greatest danger, as the deaths of Nadab and Abihu show (chapter 10). The laws exist so that the presence can stay, and the book's high point is the promise that God will make his dwelling among them and walk among them (26:11-12).

themes.title: Atonement and sacrifice
themes.body: The verb kipper, to make atonement, runs through the book. Sacrifice is more than dealing with sin: there are gifts, thanksgiving, and shared meals as well as purification and reparation. But at its center is the conviction that sin and impurity are deadly, and that God gives the blood of a substitute to cover them: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood” (17:11).

themes.title: Clean and unclean
themes.body: Impurity is a state, not always a sin. It comes from contact with death, disease, and the loss of life-fluids, and it bars a person from the sanctuary until time, washing, and sometimes an offering restore them. The system taught Israel, daily and physically, that the God of life cannot be approached casually by creatures touched by death.

themes.title: Justice, land, and neighbor
themes.body: Holiness in Leviticus is social. Farmers leave the edges of their fields for the poor and the foreigner, wages are paid the same day, the deaf and blind are protected, the foreigner is loved as oneself (19:34), and every fiftieth year land returns to its families, because “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine” (25:23).

keyChapters.why: The burnt offering, the whole gift wholly given, opens the book and introduces the laying on of hands and the language of atonement.
Nadab and Abihu die before the LORD, a stark lesson that nearness to a holy God is a gift that cannot be handled carelessly.
The food laws, the first of the clean and unclean chapters, grounded in the command to be holy because the LORD is holy.
The Day of Atonement, the book's center, with the high priest behind the veil and the scapegoat carrying sin away.
The law of blood, including the verse that explains why blood makes atonement: the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Holiness in ordinary life, from harvest to courtroom, including the command to love your neighbor as yourself.
The Sabbath year and the Jubilee, when debts, slaves, and land are released, grounded in God's ownership of the land.
The covenant's blessings and curses, ending with the promise that God will remember his covenant even in exile.
